results.answer:
The main results of the School Streets pilot evaluation were:

- **Motor traffic fell sharply on the closed streets.** Across the 12 pilot schools, traffic during restriction hours dropped from **214 to 62 vehicles per school day**, a **71% reduction**. The abstract also reports a **76% fall** during restriction hours.
- **Air pollution improved at the school gates.** Mean **NO2** at school gates fell from **31.4 ug/m3 to 26.9 ug/m3**, a **14.3% reduction**. After adjusting for background trends, the reduction attributable to the pilot was estimated at **10.6%**.
- **More pupils travelled actively.** The share of pupils who usually **walked, cycled or scooted** rose from **58% to 67%**, an increase of **9 percentage points**.
- **Some traffic was displaced to surrounding roads, but not dramatically.** Traffic on the eight boundary roads increased by **6.2%**, which the report says was within normal year-to-year variation.
- **Overall conclusion:** the pilot **reduced traffic and NO2 outside the schools with little evidence of displacement**, and the report recommends making the scheme **permanent at all 12 sites**.

ANSWER: The pilot reduced traffic and NO2 outside the 12 schools and increased active travel to school, with only limited traffic displacement to nearby roads.

results.answer:
The main results of the School Streets pilot evaluation were:

- **Motor traffic on the closed streets fell sharply** during restriction hours.
  - The report says motor traffic entering the closed streets fell **by 76% during the restriction hours** in the abstract.
  - In the detailed results, it says the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets fell from **214 to 62 per school day**, a **71% reduction** across the 12 sites.

- **Air pollution improved at the school gates.**
  - Mean **NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 ug/m3 to 26.9 ug/m3**, a **14.3% reduction**.
  - After adjusting for background changes, the reduction attributable to the pilot was estimated at **10.6%**.

- **More pupils walked, cycled or scooted to school.**
  - The share rose from **58% to 67%**, an increase of **9 percentage points**.
  - The gains were mainly among pupils living **within one kilometre** of the school.

- **Some traffic was displaced to nearby roads, but not by much overall.**
  - Traffic on the eight boundary roads increased by **6.2%**, which the report says was within normal year-to-year variation.

- **Overall conclusion:** the evaluation found that **School Streets reduced traffic and NO2 outside the pilot schools and increased active travel**, with **little evidence of harmful displacement**, and it recommended making the scheme permanent at all 12 sites.

ANSWER: The pilot mainly reduced traffic and NO2 at school gates, increased walking/cycling/scooting to school, and showed only limited traffic displacement onto nearby roads.

Evaluations/School Streets monitoring notes.md
Evaluations/School Streets pilot evaluation report.pdf
     1	School Streets Pilot Evaluation: Traffic, Air Quality and Travel to School
     2	Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford
     3	Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street
     6	outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted
     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.
   140	Table 3. Usual mode of travel to school, percentage of pupils, 10 schools
   141	Mode Baseline March 2024 Pilot March 2025
   142	Walk 49 55
   143	Cycle 3 5
   144	Scooter 6 7
   145	Car 34 25
   146	Bus 6 6
   147	Other 2 2
   148	Parents who had stopped driving most often said that the closure made walking feel safer or
   149	that parking near the school had become more difficult. Some parents reported parking
   150	further away and walking the last part of the journey, which the survey recorded as walking.
   151	
   152	4.5 Traffic on boundary roads
   153	Some drivers who previously used the closed streets diverted to the surrounding main roads.
   154	Across the eight boundary roads, traffic during the restriction hours increased by 6.2%
   155	compared with the baseline period. However, this increase was within the range of normal
   156	year-to-year variation recorded at the borough's permanent traffic counters, which is plus
   157	or minus 8%.
   158	The largest increase, 11%, was on Mill Road next to Crossley Road Primary, where the closed
   159	street had previously carried the most traffic. Outside the restriction hours, traffic on
   160	the boundary roads was unchanged.
   161	4.6 Views of parents and residents
   162	The online survey received 1,206 responses from parents and 388 from residents. Among
   163	parents, 73% supported making the School Street at their child's school permanent, and 18%
   164	were opposed. Among residents, 54% supported a permanent scheme and 37% were opposed.
   165	The resident survey had a response rate of 23%, so these results may not reflect the views
   166	of all residents. Residents who opposed the scheme most often mentioned difficulty with
   167	deliveries and visitors, while supporters most often mentioned quieter streets.
   168	4.7 Enforcement
   169	Penalty charge notices were issued throughout the pilot, but most were issued in the first
   170	half term, and the number fell steadily as drivers became familiar with the closures.
   171	Exemption permits were most often held by residents of the closed streets.
   172	
   173	5 Discussion
   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions
   194	among pupils, and the pilot period was too short to assess changes in road traffic
   195	collisions. The travel survey relied on pupils' reports of their usual mode of travel and
   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.
   204	Acknowledgements
   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each
   207	month.
   208	Funding
   209	The evaluation was funded by a grant from the Regional Active Travel Fund. The funder had no
   210	role in the design of the evaluation, the analysis or the decision to publish.
   211	References
   212	Abbott J (2020). Changing the school run: results from a 22-school programme. Urban Mobility
   213	Review 6: 100-112.
   214	Daley R, Moss K (2023). Public support for School Streets: a review of 14 evaluations. Urban
   215	Mobility Review 9: 44-58.
   216	Kerrigan P, Shaw L, Udeh C (2022). Traffic displacement near School Streets in northern
   217	England. Transport Policy Studies 31: 210-224.
   218	Pereira A, Lund M (2022). Volunteer-staffed and camera-enforced school streets compared.
   219	Local Transport Research 7: 15-29.
   220	Rowland S, Tait H (2021). Air quality at the school gate: evidence from 37 School Streets.

results.answer:
The main results of the School Streets pilot evaluation were:

- **Motor traffic outside the schools fell sharply.**  
  Vehicles entering the closed streets during restriction hours dropped from **214 to 62 per school day**, a **71% reduction**. The abstract reports this as **76%** during restriction hours, but the results section gives the school-day average reduction of **71%**.

- **Air quality improved at the school gates.**  
  Mean **NO2** at the school gates fell from **31.4 µg/m3 to 26.9 µg/m3**, a **14.3% reduction**. After adjusting for wider borough trends, the reduction attributable to the pilot was estimated at **10.6%**.

- **More children travelled actively to school.**  
  The share of pupils who usually **walked, cycled or scooted** rose from **58% to 67%**. Car use fell from **34% to 25%** in the survey sample.

- **Displacement to nearby roads was limited.**  
  Traffic on boundary roads increased by **6.2%** during restriction hours, but this was within normal year-to-year variation and **NO2 on boundary roads was essentially unchanged**.

- **Parents and residents were mostly supportive.**  
  **73% of parents** supported making the scheme permanent, and **54% of residents** were in favour.

- **Overall conclusion and recommendation:**  
  The evaluation concluded that School Streets **reduced traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools**, encouraged more active travel, and showed **little evidence of harmful traffic displacement**. It recommended making the scheme **permanent at all 12 schools** and extending it to other suitable schools.

ANSWER: The pilot significantly reduced traffic outside the schools, lowered NO2 at the school gates, increased walking/cycling/scooting to school, and showed only limited displacement to nearby roads; the report recommends making School Streets permanent at all 12 pilot schools.

Yes. The report says the road closures reduced pollution outside the schools:

- “Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of 14.3%.”

So, yes — the air outside school was cleaner for kids during drop-off, though the improvement was moderate rather than dramatic, and the report couldn’t directly measure children’s personal exposure.

     2	Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford
     3	Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street
     6	outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted
     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction

   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions
   194	among pupils, and the pilot period was too short to assess changes in road traffic
   195	collisions. The travel survey relied on pupils' reports of their usual mode of travel and
   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.
   204	Acknowledgements
   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each
   207	month.
   208	Funding
   209	The evaluation was funded by a grant from the Regional Active Travel Fund. The funder had no
   210	role in the design of the evaluation, the analysis or the decision to publish.
   211	References
   212	Abbott J (2020). Changing the school run: results from a 22-school programme. Urban Mobility
   213	Review 6: 100-112.
   214	Daley R, Moss K (2023). Public support for School Streets: a review of 14 evaluations. Urban
   215	Mobility Review 9: 44-58.

   217	England. Transport Policy Studies 31: 210-224.

   220	Rowland S, Tait H (2021). Air quality at the school gate: evidence from 37 School Streets.
   221	City Air Quality Journal 4: 77-90.
   222	Data availability
   223	Anonymised traffic counts and diffusion tube results are available from the Transport Policy
   224	and Research Team on request.
   225	Appendix A. Pilot schools
   226	
   227	The 12 pilot schools were Ashgrove Primary, Beckside Primary, Crossley Road Primary, Dunmore
   228	Infant School, Elmfield Primary, Fairholme Junior School, Greystone Primary, Hollins Lane
   229	Primary, Ivydale Primary, Juniper Hill Primary, Kingsmead Primary and Larkrise Primary.

     2	Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford
     3	Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street
     6	outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted
     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.
   140	Table 3. Usual mode of travel to school, percentage of pupils, 10 schools
   141	Mode Baseline March 2024 Pilot March 2025
   142	Walk 49 55
   143	Cycle 3 5
   144	Scooter 6 7
   145	Car 34 25
   146	Bus 6 6
   147	Other 2 2
   148	Parents who had stopped driving most often said that the closure made walking feel safer or
   149	that parking near the school had become more difficult. Some parents reported parking
   150	further away and walking the last part of the journey, which the survey recorded as walking.
   151	
   152	4.5 Traffic on boundary roads
   153	Some drivers who previously used the closed streets diverted to the surrounding main roads.
   154	Across the eight boundary roads, traffic during the restriction hours increased by 6.2%
   155	compared with the baseline period. However, this increase was within the range of normal
   156	year-to-year variation recorded at the borough's permanent traffic counters, which is plus
   157	or minus 8%.
   158	The largest increase, 11%, was on Mill Road next to Crossley Road Primary, where the closed
   159	street had previously carried the most traffic. Outside the restriction hours, traffic on
   160	the boundary roads was unchanged.
   161	4.6 Views of parents and residents
   162	The online survey received 1,206 responses from parents and 388 from residents. Among
   163	parents, 73% supported making the School Street at their child's school permanent, and 18%
   164	were opposed. Among residents, 54% supported a permanent scheme and 37% were opposed.
   165	The resident survey had a response rate of 23%, so these results may not reflect the views
   166	of all residents. Residents who opposed the scheme most often mentioned difficulty with
   167	deliveries and visitors, while supporters most often mentioned quieter streets.
   168	4.7 Enforcement
   169	Penalty charge notices were issued throughout the pilot, but most were issued in the first
   170	half term, and the number fell steadily as drivers became familiar with the closures.
   171	Exemption permits were most often held by residents of the closed streets.
   172	
   173	5 Discussion
   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions

   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.

   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each

     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.
   140	Table 3. Usual mode of travel to school, percentage of pupils, 10 schools
   141	Mode Baseline March 2024 Pilot March 2025
   142	Walk 49 55
   143	Cycle 3 5
   144	Scooter 6 7
   145	Car 34 25
   146	Bus 6 6
   147	Other 2 2
   148	Parents who had stopped driving most often said that the closure made walking feel safer or
   149	that parking near the school had become more difficult. Some parents reported parking
   150	further away and walking the last part of the journey, which the survey recorded as walking.
   151	
   152	4.5 Traffic on boundary roads
   153	Some drivers who previously used the closed streets diverted to the surrounding main roads.
   154	Across the eight boundary roads, traffic during the restriction hours increased by 6.2%
   155	compared with the baseline period. However, this increase was within the range of normal
   156	year-to-year variation recorded at the borough's permanent traffic counters, which is plus
   157	or minus 8%.
   158	The largest increase, 11%, was on Mill Road next to Crossley Road Primary, where the closed
   159	street had previously carried the most traffic. Outside the restriction hours, traffic on
   160	the boundary roads was unchanged.
   161	4.6 Views of parents and residents
   162	The online survey received 1,206 responses from parents and 388 from residents. Among
   163	parents, 73% supported making the School Street at their child's school permanent, and 18%
   164	were opposed. Among residents, 54% supported a permanent scheme and 37% were opposed.
   165	The resident survey had a response rate of 23%, so these results may not reflect the views
   166	of all residents. Residents who opposed the scheme most often mentioned difficulty with
   167	deliveries and visitors, while supporters most often mentioned quieter streets.
   168	4.7 Enforcement
   169	Penalty charge notices were issued throughout the pilot, but most were issued in the first
   170	half term, and the number fell steadily as drivers became familiar with the closures.
   171	Exemption permits were most often held by residents of the closed streets.
   172	
   173	5 Discussion
   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions
   194	among pupils, and the pilot period was too short to assess changes in road traffic
   195	collisions. The travel survey relied on pupils' reports of their usual mode of travel and
   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.
   204	Acknowledgements
   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each
   207	month.
   208	Funding
   209	The evaluation was funded by a grant from the Regional Active Travel Fund. The funder had no
   210	role in the design of the evaluation, the analysis or the decision to publish.
   211	References
   212	Abbott J (2020). Changing the school run: results from a 22-school programme. Urban Mobility
   213	Review 6: 100-112.
   214	Daley R, Moss K (2023). Public support for School Streets: a review of 14 evaluations. Urban
   215	Mobility Review 9: 44-58.
   216	Kerrigan P, Shaw L, Udeh C (2022). Traffic displacement near School Streets in northern
   217	England. Transport Policy Studies 31: 210-224.
   218	Pereira A, Lund M (2022). Volunteer-staffed and camera-enforced school streets compared.
   219	Local Transport Research 7: 15-29.
   220	Rowland S, Tait H (2021). Air quality at the school gate: evidence from 37 School Streets.
   221	City Air Quality Journal 4: 77-90.
   222	Data availability
   223	Anonymised traffic counts and diffusion tube results are available from the Transport Policy
   224	and Research Team on request.
   225	Appendix A. Pilot schools
   226	
   227	The 12 pilot schools were Ashgrove Primary, Beckside Primary, Crossley Road Primary, Dunmore
   228	Infant School, Elmfield Primary, Fairholme Junior School, Greystone Primary, Hollins Lane
   229	Primary, Ivydale Primary, Juniper Hill Primary, Kingsmead Primary and Larkrise Primary.
   230	Site-level traffic and NO2 results are held in the accompanying site data workbook.
results.answer:
Yes. The report says the share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school “rose from 58% in the baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey,” a gain of 9 percentage points. It also says the scheme was “associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school.”

ANSWER: Yes — the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school rose from 58% to 67% (up 9 percentage points).
