     1	Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards: A Stepped-Wedge Evaluation
     2	Evaluation report, September 2025. Department of Nursing Research and Practice Development,
     3	Calderbrook General Hospital.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen
     6	hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions. We evaluated a
     7	nurse-led discharge planning model on six acute medical wards.
     8	Methods. The model combined a dedicated discharge coordinator nurse on each ward, an
     9	expected date of discharge set within 24 hours of admission, daily board rounds and
    10	criteria-led discharge. Wards moved from usual care to the new model in a stepped-wedge
    11	sequence between April 2024 and March 2025. The primary outcome was length of stay.
    12	Results. The evaluation included 6,948 admissions. Mean length of stay fell from 7.9 to 7.1
    13	days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days. Emergency readmission within 30 days was slightly
    14	lower in the intervention period, and more patients left hospital before noon.
    15	Conclusions. Nurse-led discharge planning shortened hospital stays without an increase in
    16	readmissions or deaths. The model could be extended to other wards.
    17	
    18	1 Introduction
    19	Calderbrook General Hospital has operated at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the
    20	past three years. On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients
    21	who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at
    22	home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the
    23	emergency department.
    24	National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set
    25	an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the
    26	day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers
    27	and medical teams and were not sustained.
    28	In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a
    29	dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the
    30	day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical
    31	wards over twelve months.
    32	2 Literature review
    33	Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow
    34	and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7
    35	days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30
    36	days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge
    37	reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with
    38	emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.
    39	Other studies have focused on the timing of discharge. Lindqvist (2021) found that the share
    40	of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were
    41	introduced in a teaching hospital. The workload implications are less clear: Prescott (2019)
    42	estimated that nurse-led discharge required 31 minutes of additional registered nurse time
    43	per patient, while Haddad and Byrne (2022) found no change in overtime hours.
    44	Few studies have evaluated a combined model in a district general hospital, and fewer still
    45	have measured both patient outcomes and nursing time.
    46	
    47	3 Methods
    48	3.1 Setting and design
    49	The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds. We used a
    50	stepped-wedge design: all wards began in the control period, and one ward moved to the
    51	intervention every two months, in an order chosen by lottery, until all six wards were using
    52	the new model.
    53	3.2 The intervention
    54	Each ward appointed a discharge coordinator, a band 6 registered nurse working on weekdays,
    55	funded at 1.0 whole-time equivalent per ward. The coordinator set an expected date of
    56	discharge within 24 hours of admission, led a daily board round at 09:00, arranged
    57	medicines, transport and community referrals, and authorised criteria-led discharge when
    58	agreed clinical criteria were met. Ward managers and coordinators received two half-day
    59	training sessions before each ward moved to the intervention.
    60	3.3 Outcomes
    61	The primary outcome was length of stay in days. Secondary outcomes were emergency
    62	readmission within 30 days, death within 30 days of discharge, the proportion of patients
    63	discharged before noon, and bed-days lost to delayed discharge. Patients completed a
    64	readiness for discharge questionnaire, scored from 0 to 10, on the day of discharge.
    65	Nursing time was measured by work sampling on two randomly chosen days each month. Ward
    66	staff nurses were invited to complete an anonymous workload survey in March 2025.
    67	3.4 Analysis
    68	Outcomes were compared between control and intervention periods using mixed-effects models
    69	with a random effect for ward and a fixed effect for calendar month, to allow for seasonal
    70	trends. Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of
    71	0.05 was specified in advance.
    72	3.5 Data sources
    73	Admission, discharge and readmission data were taken from the hospital's patient
    74	administration system. Deaths after discharge were identified through the national death
    75	register, and delayed discharges were taken from the daily ward status return.
    76	3.6 Patient and public involvement
    77	
    78	Two former patients and a carer sat on the evaluation steering group. They helped to word
    79	the readiness for discharge questionnaire and advised on how to approach patients on the day
    80	of discharge.
    81	
    82	4 Results
    83	4.1 Participants
    84	The evaluation included 6,948 admissions of adults aged 18 and over: 3,302 during control
    85	periods and 3,646 during intervention periods. Patient characteristics were similar in the
    86	two periods (Table 1).
    87	Table 1. Characteristics of admissions by study period
    88	Characteristic Control period Intervention period
    89	Admissions 3,302 3,646
    90	Mean age, years 74.1 73.8
    91	Women, % 52 51
    92	Admitted through the emergency department, % 88 89
    93	Living alone, % 34 33
    94	Aged 80 and over, % 32 32
    95	4.2 Length of stay
    96	Mean length of stay was 7.9 days in the control period and 7.1 days in the intervention
    97	period. After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of
    98	stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1). Table 2 summarises the primary and secondary outcomes.
    99	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by study period
   100	Outcome Control period Intervention period Adjusted effect (95% CI)
   101	Mean length of stay, days 7.9 7.1 -0.8 days (-1.1 to -0.5)
   102	Emergency readmission within 30 days, % 15.1 14.2 OR 0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)
   103	Discharged before noon, % 18.6 29.3 OR 1.84 (1.58 to 2.14)
   104	Death within 30 days of discharge, % 5.4 5.2 OR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18)
   105	Readiness for discharge score, 0 to 10 6.8 7.4 +0.6 (0.3 to 0.9)
   106	
   107	4.3 Readmissions and mortality
   108	Emergency readmission within 30 days occurred after 14.2% of discharges in the intervention
   109	period and 15.1% of discharges in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.79
   110	to 1.09). However, the difference was not statistically significant. Mortality within 30
   111	days of discharge was similar in the two periods (Table 2). The most common reasons for
   112	readmission in both periods were respiratory infection, heart failure and urinary infection.
   113	4.4 Discharge timing and delays
   114	The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2).
   115	Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically
   116	fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This
   117	fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport.
   118	4.5 Readiness for discharge
   119	Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital.
   120	The mean readiness for discharge score rose from 6.8 to 7.4 out of 10. Questionnaires were
   121	returned by 61% of patients, and the return rate was lower among patients aged 80 and over.
   122	
   123	4.6 Results by age group
   124	The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and
   125	over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost
   126	three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days.
   127	The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol.
   128	Table 3. Mean length of stay in days by age group and study period
   129	Age group Control period Intervention period Difference
   130	18 to 64 5.6 5.3 -0.3
   131	65 to 79 7.6 6.9 -0.7
   132	80 and over 10.4 9.0 -1.4
   133	All ages 7.9 7.1 -0.8
   134	Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the
   135	control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent
   136	waiting for care packages at home.
   137	
   138	4.7 Nursing time and workload
   139	Work sampling showed that discharge coordinators spent a mean of 26 minutes on each
   140	discharge, covering board rounds, referrals, medicines and contact with families. Time spent
   141	by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from 52 to 34 minutes per shift.
   142	In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or
   143	lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier. Only 41% of ward nurses
   144	returned the survey, so these views may not be representative of all ward staff.
   145	4.8 Implementation
   146	An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the
   147	intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays. Criteria-led discharge
   148	was used for 19% of discharges, most often at weekends when no senior doctor was on the
   149	ward.
   150	5 Discussion
   151	The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier
   152	trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most
   153	bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths.
   154	The reduction of 0.8 days is close to the 0.7 days reported in the review by Marlow and Ince
   155	(2018), and larger than the 0.5 days found for criteria-led discharge alone by Okafor and
   156	colleagues (2020). The rise in discharges before noon was larger than in earlier reports,
   157	which suggests that the daily board round was an important part of the model.
   158	The workload findings need careful interpretation. The time saved by ward staff nurses was
   159	largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators, so the model redistributed discharge
   160	work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.
   161	
   162	6 Limitations
   163	This was a single-site evaluation, and ward staff could not be blinded to the intervention.
   164	Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of
   165	seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may
   166	have contributed to shorter stays. We did not undertake an economic evaluation, so the costs
   167	of the coordinator posts have not been compared with the value of the bed-days saved.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay on acute medical wards without
   170	increasing readmissions. The hospital should consider extending the model to the remaining
   171	medical wards, with continued monitoring of readmissions and staff workload.
   172	Acknowledgements
   173	We thank the ward managers, discharge coordinators and patients who took part, and the
   174	hospital's information team for extracting admission data.
   175	Ethics and data availability
   176	The evaluation was registered as a service evaluation with the hospital's clinical audit
   177	department, and research ethics committee review was not required. Patients could decline
   178	the readiness questionnaire without any effect on their care. Aggregate data are available
   179	from the Department of Nursing Research on request.
   180	Funding and conflicts of interest
   181	The evaluation was funded by the Calderbrook Hospital Charity. The authors are employed by
   182	the hospital, and two of the authors helped to design the nurse-led model.
   183	References
   184	Haddad N, Byrne S (2022). Overtime and discharge planning on medical wards. Nursing
   185	Workforce Journal 12: 88-97.
   186	Lindqvist E (2021). Board rounds and the timing of hospital discharge. Hospital Flow
   187	Quarterly 5: 31-40.
   188	Marlow T, Ince G (2018). Structured discharge planning: a review of 30 randomised trials.
   189	Review of Hospital Care 22: 140-161.
   190	Okafor U, Brennan J, Silva M (2020). Criteria-led discharge in eight hospitals: a cluster
   191	
   192	trial. Acute Medicine Research 14: 201-213.
   193	Prescott D (2019). Measuring the nursing time cost of discharge. Journal of Ward Practice 9:
   194	57-66.
     1	Board Briefing: Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards
     2	
     3	For the Trust Board meeting on 6 November 2025. Prepared by the Office of the Chief Nurse. For decision.
     4	
     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This paper summarises the evaluation of the nurse-led discharge planning model that ran on six acute medical wards between April 2024 and March 2025, and asks the Board to approve extending the model.
     8	
     9	Background
    10	
    11	The acute medical wards have run at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the last three years, and delays in discharge are a major cause of long waits for beds in the emergency department. The nurse-led model was designed to plan each discharge from the day of admission, with a dedicated coordinator nurse on every ward.
    12	
    13	Key findings
    14	
    15	The evaluation covered 6,948 admissions. Under the new model, the average hospital stay was 1.2 days shorter, which is equivalent to freeing several beds every day across the six wards.
    16	
    17	Readmissions within 30 days fell from 15.1% to 14.2%, and patients reported feeling better prepared to go home. Patients aged 80 and over benefited most.
    18	
    19	Ward nurses now spend less time on discharge paperwork, and most nurses who responded to the staff survey said their workload was the same or lighter.
    20	
    21	Resources
    22	
    23	The model requires one discharge coordinator nurse per ward. The six coordinator posts are funded from the hospital charity grant until March 2026. No savings have yet been calculated, and Finance will develop the economic case for the Board in early 2026.
    24	
    25	Recommendation
    26	
    27	The Board is asked to approve extending nurse-led discharge planning to the four remaining medical wards from April 2026, subject to the economic case.
    28	
    29	Risks
    30	
    31	The main risks are recruiting experienced band 6 nurses to the coordinator posts and keeping daily board rounds going during periods of high demand.
    32	
    33	Next steps
    34	
    35	If the Board approves the extension, recruitment to the four new coordinator posts will begin in January 2026, and the Chief Nurse will report progress to the Quality Committee every quarter.
results.answer:
Yes. The subgroup analysis showed a bigger reduction for the very old patients:

- Among patients aged 80 years and over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days.
- For patients under 80, the reduction was 0.5 days.

The report says, “This effect was almost three times the reduction seen in patients under 80,” and the board briefing also says, “Patients aged 80 and over benefited most.”

ANSWER: Yes — the effect was larger for patients aged 80 and over, with length of stay falling by 1.4 days versus 0.5 days in younger patients.

  p.1 §Abstract: "Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions." #MBZA5PTKM0
  p.2 §1 Introduction: "On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at home." #574YFY6NEN
  p.2 §2 Literature review: "Lindqvist (2021) found that the share of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were introduced in a teaching hospital." #NE15P4MHZ2
  p.3 §3.1 Setting and design: "The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds." #RWCZT6Q2BX
  p.3 §3.4 Analysis: "Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of 0.05 was specified in advance." #R3X17Y66Q3
  p.5 §4.1 Participants: "Patient characteristics were similar in the two periods (Table 1)." #3QK3NNSZ21
  p.5 §4.2 Length of stay: "After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1)." #9QYRM2QJMC
  p.6 §4.4 Discharge timing and delays: "The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2). Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport." #V8JMZF6A4C
  p.6 §4.5 Readiness for discharge: "Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital." #K0813VNGFT
  p.7 §4.6 Results by age group: "The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days. The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol." #4S6GPKQ6WN
  p.7: "Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent waiting for care packages at home." #T7KCCRVXH5
  p.8 §4.7 Nursing time and workload: "In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier." #BW4E8Q4M99
  p.8 §4.8 Implementation: "An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays." #JX7NJPTKQ9
  p.8 §5 Discussion: "The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths." #MJ8FFFJ1GE
  p.9 §6 Limitations: "Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may have contributed to shorter stays." #7Z2NAH46SW

     1	Board Briefing: Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards
     2	
     3	For the Trust Board meeting on 6 November 2025. Prepared by the Office of the Chief Nurse. For decision.
     4	
     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This paper summarises the evaluation of the nurse-led discharge planning model that ran on six acute medical wards between April 2024 and March 2025, and asks the Board to approve extending the model.
     8	
     9	Background
    10	
    11	The acute medical wards have run at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the last three years, and delays in discharge are a major cause of long waits for beds in the emergency department. The nurse-led model was designed to plan each discharge from the day of admission, with a dedicated coordinator nurse on every ward.
    12	
    13	Key findings
    14	
    15	The evaluation covered 6,948 admissions. Under the new model, the average hospital stay was 1.2 days shorter, which is equivalent to freeing several beds every day across the six wards.
    16	
    17	Readmissions within 30 days fell from 15.1% to 14.2%, and patients reported feeling better prepared to go home. Patients aged 80 and over benefited most.
    18

     1	Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards: A Stepped-Wedge Evaluation
     2	Evaluation report, September 2025. Department of Nursing Research and Practice Development,
     3	Calderbrook General Hospital.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen
     6	hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions. We evaluated a
     7	nurse-led discharge planning model on six acute medical wards.
     8	Methods. The model combined a dedicated discharge coordinator nurse on each ward, an
     9	expected date of discharge set within 24 hours of admission, daily board rounds and
    10	criteria-led discharge. Wards moved from usual care to the new model in a stepped-wedge
    11	sequence between April 2024 and March 2025. The primary outcome was length of stay.
    12	Results. The evaluation included 6,948 admissions. Mean length of stay fell from 7.9 to 7.1
    13	days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days. Emergency readmission within 30 days was slightly
    14	lower in the intervention period, and more patients left hospital before noon.
    15	Conclusions. Nurse-led discharge planning shortened hospital stays without an increase in
    16	readmissions or deaths. The model could be extended to other wards.
    17	
    18	1 Introduction
    19	Calderbrook General Hospital has operated at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the
    20	past three years. On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients
    21	who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at
    22	home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the
    23	emergency department.
    24	National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set
    25	an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the
    26	day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers
    27	and medical teams and were not sustained.
    28	In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a
    29	dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the
    30	day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical
    31	wards over twelve months.
    32	2 Literature review
    33	Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow
    34	and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7
    35	days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30
    36	days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge
    37	reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with
    38	emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.
    39	Other studies have focused on the timing of discharge. Lindqvist (2021) found that the share
    40	of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were
    41	introduced in a teaching hospital. The workload implications are less clear: Prescott (2019)
    42	estimated that nurse-led discharge required 31 minutes of additional registered nurse time
    43	per patient, while Haddad and Byrne (2022) found no change in overtime hours.
    44	Few studies have evaluated a combined model in a district general hospital, and fewer still
    45	have measured both patient outcomes and nursing time.
    46	
    47	3 Methods
    48	3.1 Setting and design
    49	The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds. We used a
    50	stepped-wedge design: all wards began in the control period, and one ward moved to the
    51	intervention every two months, in an order chosen by lottery, until all six wards were using
    52	the new model.
    53	3.2 The intervention
    54	Each ward appointed a discharge coordinator, a band 6 registered nurse working on weekdays,
    55	funded at 1.0 whole-time equivalent per ward. The coordinator set an expected date of
    56	discharge within 24 hours of admission, led a daily board round at 09:00, arranged
    57	medicines, transport and community referrals, and authorised criteria-led discharge when
    58	agreed clinical criteria were met. Ward managers and coordinators received two half-day
    59	training sessions before each ward moved to the intervention.
    60	3.3 Outcomes
    61	The primary outcome was length of stay in days. Secondary outcomes were emergency
    62	readmission within 30 days, death within 30 days of discharge, the proportion of patients
    63	discharged before noon, and bed-days lost to delayed discharge. Patients completed a
    64	readiness for discharge questionnaire, scored from 0 to 10, on the day of discharge.
    65	Nursing time was measured by work sampling on two randomly chosen days each month. Ward
    66	staff nurses were invited to complete an anonymous workload survey in March 2025.
    67	3.4 Analysis
    68	Outcomes were compared between control and intervention periods using mixed-effects models
    69	with a random effect for ward and a fixed effect for calendar month, to allow for seasonal
    70	trends. Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of
    71	0.05 was specified in advance.
    72	3.5 Data sources
    73	Admission, discharge and readmission data were taken from the hospital's patient
    74	administration system. Deaths after discharge were identified through the national death
    75	register, and delayed discharges were taken from the daily ward status return.
    76	3.6 Patient and public involvement
    77	
    78	Two former patients and a carer sat on the evaluation steering group. They helped to word
    79	the readiness for discharge questionnaire and advised on how to approach patients on the day
    80	of discharge.
    81	
    82	4 Results
    83	4.1 Participants
    84	The evaluation included 6,948 admissions of adults aged 18 and over: 3,302 during control
    85	periods and 3,646 during intervention periods. Patient characteristics were similar in the
    86	two periods (Table 1).
    87	Table 1. Characteristics of admissions by study period
    88	Characteristic Control period Intervention period
    89	Admissions 3,302 3,646
    90	Mean age, years 74.1 73.8
    91	Women, % 52 51
    92	Admitted through the emergency department, % 88 89
    93	Living alone, % 34 33
    94	Aged 80 and over, % 32 32
    95	4.2 Length of stay
    96	Mean length of stay was 7.9 days in the control period and 7.1 days in the intervention
    97	period. After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of
    98	stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1). Table 2 summarises the primary and secondary outcomes.
    99	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by study period
   100	Outcome Control period Intervention period Adjusted effect (95% CI)
   101	Mean length of stay, days 7.9 7.1 -0.8 days (-1.1 to -0.5)
   102	Emergency readmission within 30 days, % 15.1 14.2 OR 0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)
   103	Discharged before noon, % 18.6 29.3 OR 1.84 (1.58 to 2.14)
   104	Death within 30 days of discharge, % 5.4 5.2 OR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18)
   105	Readiness for discharge score, 0 to 10 6.8 7.4 +0.6 (0.3 to 0.9)
   106	
   107	4.3 Readmissions and mortality
   108	Emergency readmission within 30 days occurred after 14.2% of discharges in the intervention
   109	period and 15.1% of discharges in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.79
   110	to 1.09). However, the difference was not statistically significant. Mortality within 30
   111	days of discharge was similar in the two periods (Table 2). The most common reasons for
   112	readmission in both periods were respiratory infection, heart failure and urinary infection.
   113	4.4 Discharge timing and delays
   114	The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2).
   115	Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically
   116	fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This
   117	fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport.
   118	4.5 Readiness for discharge
   119	Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital.
   120	The mean readiness for discharge score rose from 6.8 to 7.4 out of 10. Questionnaires were
   121	returned by 61% of patients, and the return rate was lower among patients aged 80 and over.
   122	
   123	4.6 Results by age group
   124	The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and
   125	over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost
   126	three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days.
   127	The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol.
   128	Table 3. Mean length of stay in days by age group and study period
   129	Age group Control period Intervention period Difference
   130	18 to 64 5.6 5.3 -0.3
   131	65 to 79 7.6 6.9 -0.7
   132	80 and over 10.4 9.0 -1.4
   133	All ages 7.9 7.1 -0.8
   134	Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the
   135	control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent
   136	waiting for care packages at home.
   137	
   138	4.7 Nursing time and workload
   139	Work sampling showed that discharge coordinators spent a mean of 26 minutes on each
   140	discharge, covering board rounds, referrals, medicines and contact with families. Time spent
   141	by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from 52 to 34 minutes per shift.
   142	In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or
   143	lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier. Only 41% of ward nurses
   144	returned the survey, so these views may not be representative of all ward staff.
   145	4.8 Implementation
   146	An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the
   147	intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays. Criteria-led discharge
   148	was used for 19% of discharges, most often at weekends when no senior doctor was on the
   149	ward.
   150	5 Discussion
   151	The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier
   152	trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most
   153	bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths.
   154	The reduction of 0.8 days is close to the 0.7 days reported in the review by Marlow and Ince
   155	(2018), and larger than the 0.5 days found for criteria-led discharge alone by Okafor and
   156	colleagues (2020). The rise in discharges before noon was larger than in earlier reports,
   157	which suggests that the daily board round was an important part of the model.
   158	The workload findings need careful interpretation. The time saved by ward staff nurses was
   159	largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators, so the model redistributed discharge
   160	work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.
   161	
   162	6 Limitations
   163	This was a single-site evaluation, and ward staff could not be blinded to the intervention.
   164	Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of
   165	seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may
   166	have contributed to shorter stays. We did not undertake an economic evaluation, so the costs
   167	of the coordinator posts have not been compared with the value of the bed-days saved.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay on acute medical wards without
   170	increasing readmissions. The hospital should consider extending the model to the remaining
   171	medical wards, with continued monitoring of readmissions and staff workload.
   172	Acknowledgements
   173	We thank the ward managers, discharge coordinators and patients who took part, and the
   174	hospital's information team for extracting admission data.
   175	Ethics and data availability
   176	The evaluation was registered as a service evaluation with the hospital's clinical audit
   177	department, and research ethics committee review was not required. Patients could decline
   178	the readiness questionnaire without any effect on their care. Aggregate data are available
   179	from the Department of Nursing Research on request.
   180	Funding and conflicts of interest
   181	The evaluation was funded by the Calderbrook Hospital Charity. The authors are employed by
   182	the hospital, and two of the authors helped to design the nurse-led model.
   183	References
   184	Haddad N, Byrne S (2022). Overtime and discharge planning on medical wards. Nursing
   185	Workforce Journal 12: 88-97.
   186	Lindqvist E (2021). Board rounds and the timing of hospital discharge. Hospital Flow
   187	Quarterly 5: 31-40.
   188	Marlow T, Ince G (2018). Structured discharge planning: a review of 30 randomised trials.
   189	Review of Hospital Care 22: 140-161.
   190	Okafor U, Brennan J, Silva M (2020). Criteria-led discharge in eight hospitals: a cluster
   191	
   192	trial. Acute Medicine Research 14: 201-213.
   193	Prescott D (2019). Measuring the nursing time cost of discharge. Journal of Ward Practice 9:
   194	57-66.
